title: Counterfeit Ledger Nano S Plus shown by @zhongbentong7

components: One QFN chip printed with the Ledger logo and no part number, in place of Ledger's ST33 secure element and STM32 MCU
Crystal oscillator (X1), and buttons along the edge labelled S2, where the genuine board has SW1 and SW2
USB-C connector at the same end as the genuine board, with a fine-pitch display connector
Plain copper back with no test points and no Data Matrix label
implant.notes: X user @zhongbentong7 asked Mark Karpelès (@MagicalTux) to check two opened Nano S Plus boards, which they marked 1 and 2 in red. Board 1 has the parts and layout of a genuine Nano S Plus: two ST chips (the secure element and the MCU), numbered test points on the back, and a Data Matrix label. Board 2 has a different layout, built around one chip that carries a Ledger logo instead of a maker's name and part number. It has no secure element, so it can't protect a recovery phrase. Mark Karpelès replied that the second device is a known fake, which Ledger Wallet rejects as not genuine. It's a fake device, not an implant added to a genuine one. It's the same counterfeit board that Cos (@evilcos) opened the day before. The post doesn't say where either device was bought.

images.caption: Board 2, the fake: one chip printed with the Ledger logo where the part markings should be, and a crystal (X1), with the USB-C connector on the right.
Board 2 from the back, still attached to its display: plain traces, with no test points and no Data Matrix label.
For comparison, board 1 from the same post, which looks genuine: two ST chips, the secure element and the MCU.
Board 1 from the back: numbered test points (TP1 to TP29), the display connector (J1) and a Data Matrix label.
